note: Lower-48 park kits for the virtual map picker. Default tour is the Maine-to-Rockies road. Custom maps hide the road and pin parks at true lat/lon. Films skip title cards (video.start) so autoplay opens on the iconic shot. Alaska, Hawaii, and territories omitted — they do not sit on this CONUS SVG.

cards.label: Acadia
cards.blurb: Cadillac views and coast loops — timed entry often needed for the summit road.
cards.challenge: Why is ocean water salty? What happens when waves hit rock?
cards.printAnswer: Rivers carry a little salt from rocks, and it stays in the sea. Waves slowly wear the rock away.

cards.label: Great Smoky Mountains
cards.blurb: Sugarlands side — visitor center, easy forest paths, waterfall stop.
cards.challenge: Why do faraway mountains look blue or smoky?
cards.printAnswer: Air and tiny drops scatter light, so far ridges look blue or hazy.

cards.label: Everglades
cards.blurb: Anhinga / boardwalk wildlife — short wetland loop, not the whole 'Glades.
cards.challenge: Why is a wetland so important? Who lives in the sawgrass?
cards.printAnswer: Wetlands clean water and make a home for birds, fish, and gators. Sawgrass is a wet prairie, not a dry field.

video.title: Alligators and wildlife of the Everglades

cards.label: Big Bend
cards.blurb: Big Bend — desert mountains and Rio Grande; pick one short area, not the whole park.
cards.challenge: How can a river cut through a desert? Where does the water go?
cards.printAnswer: Even a dry place can have a strong river. The water carved the land for a long time and keeps flowing on.

video.title: Big Bend Chisos mountains and canyons

cards.label: Grand Canyon
cards.blurb: South Rim village — rail overlooks and a short rim walk, not the whole canyon.
cards.challenge: How did a river cut a canyon this deep?
cards.printAnswer: The Colorado River wore away rock, grain by grain, for millions of years. Slow water can cut a huge canyon.

cam.camLabel: Grand Canyon webcams · National Park Service

cards.label: Yosemite
cards.blurb: Yosemite Valley icons — falls, meadow, and Half Dome from the floor.
cards.challenge: How does a waterfall start? Why is granite so steep?
cards.printAnswer: A river falls where the land drops. Ice and rock-cracking made the granite walls steep.

cards.label: Olympic
cards.blurb: Olympic — pick one: rainforest, coast, or hurricane ridge — not all three.
cards.challenge: Why can one park have rain forest and ocean?
cards.printAnswer: Mountains catch wet air from the sea. One side stays rainy and green; the coast stays wild and salty.

cards.label: Glacier
cards.blurb: Glacier — short valley or lake stops; Going-to-the-Sun is seasonal.
cards.challenge: Why is glacier ice blue? How does a glacier move?
cards.printAnswer: Thick ice swallows other colors and lets blue through. The ice is a slow river — it slides under its own weight.

cards.label: Yellowstone
cards.blurb: Old Faithful area — geysers, boardwalks, and one finishable basin loop.
cards.challenge: Why does a geyser shoot up? What’s under the ground?
cards.printAnswer: Water soaks down, hits hot rock, and blasts out as steam. A huge heat source sits under the park.

cards.label: Rocky Mountain
cards.blurb: Beaver Meadows / easy alpine views — altitude-aware half day.
cards.challenge: Why is it harder to breathe up high? Why are mountains snowy?
cards.printAnswer: The air is thinner up high, so each breath has less oxygen. It stays colder, so snow can last.

cam.camLabel: Rocky Mountain webcams · National Park Service

cards.label: Arches
cards.blurb: Windows / Delicate area — short desert loops and iconic arches.
cards.challenge: How does a rock become an arch?
cards.printAnswer: Softer rock underneath wears away first. The harder rock on top stays, and a window opens.

cards.label: Badlands
cards.blurb: Badlands — loop road overlooks and a short fossil/boardwalk stop.
cards.challenge: Why are the hills striped with color?
cards.printAnswer: Each stripe is a different layer of old mud and ash. Wind and rain cut them into sharp hills.

cards.label: Biscayne
cards.blurb: Biscayne — mostly water; visitor center and jetty/shore when not on a boat.
cards.challenge: Why is the water so blue-green here?
cards.printAnswer: Shallow water over sand and coral lets light bounce back. The sea is a home, not just a swimming pool.

cards.label: Black Canyon
cards.blurb: Black Canyon — South Rim overlooks; stay behind rails on sheer drops.
cards.challenge: Why is this canyon so dark and skinny?
cards.printAnswer: Hard rock and a fast river cut down more than they cut sideways. Sunlight barely reaches the bottom.

video.title: Black Canyon of the Gunnison walls

cards.label: Bryce Canyon
cards.blurb: Rim overlooks of orange hoodoos — skip the full amphitheater hike for little kids.
cards.challenge: What are hoodoos? How do they stand up?
cards.printAnswer: Hoodoos are skinny rock towers. Ice and rain nibble the sides but leave a harder cap on top.

cards.label: Canyonlands
cards.blurb: Canyonlands — Island in the Sky overlooks; one mesa, not all districts.
cards.challenge: Why do rivers make such a maze of canyons?
cards.printAnswer: Two rivers cut down through stacked rock. Side washes join in, so the land looks like a puzzle.

cards.label: Capitol Reef
cards.blurb: Capitol Reef — orchard valley and red cliffs; short scenic drive stops.
cards.challenge: What is a fold in the earth?
cards.printAnswer: Layers of rock got pushed and bent like a rug. The fold makes cliffs, domes, and a wrinkle you can see.

cards.label: Carlsbad
cards.blurb: Carlsbad — Big Room cave (self-guided or tour) and visitor center.
cards.challenge: How does a cave get so huge underground?
cards.printAnswer: Water dissolved limestone for a very long time. Drips built stone icicles after the rooms were hollow.

video.title: Carlsbad Caverns Big Room — no talking

cards.label: Channel Is.
cards.blurb: Channel Islands — mainland visitor center if not on a boat day.
cards.challenge: Why do islands have animals you don’t see on the mainland?
cards.printAnswer: Water isolates them. Animals change over time when they can’t mix with the shore.

cards.label: Congaree
cards.blurb: Congaree — boardwalk through old-growth bottomland forest.
cards.challenge: Why are these trees so tall in a swamp?
cards.printAnswer: Floods bring rich mud. The trees drink it and race upward for light.

cards.label: Crater Lake
cards.blurb: Crater Lake — rim overlooks of the deep blue caldera; rim drive seasonal.
cards.challenge: How did a lake get inside a mountain?
cards.printAnswer: A volcano collapsed and left a bowl. Rain and snow filled it with very deep, clear water.

cards.label: Cuyahoga
cards.blurb: Near-city towpath day — flat canal path and easy nature stops.
cards.challenge: How can a river park sit next to a city?
cards.printAnswer: The river kept a wild strip. Trails and a towpath follow water that carved the valley.

cards.label: Death Valley
cards.blurb: Death Valley — short cool-season stops only; heat is the limit.
cards.challenge: Why is this one of the hottest, lowest places?
cards.printAnswer: Mountains trap heat and dry air. The floor sits below sea level, so heat piles up.

cards.label: Dry Tortugas
cards.blurb: Dry Tortugas — ferry or seaplane day to Fort Jefferson; plan transit first.
cards.challenge: Why is there a huge brick fort in the ocean?
cards.printAnswer: Ships needed a lookout. Builders used an island of coral and sand far from the mainland.

cards.label: Gateway Arch
cards.blurb: Gateway Arch — riverfront park and arch grounds; tram tickets separate.
cards.challenge: Why is the Arch a giant curve?
cards.printAnswer: A catenary curve is strong — like a chain hanging, flipped up. It marks the river gateway.

cards.label: Grand Teton
cards.blurb: Grand Teton — mountain backdrop pullouts and Jenny Lake area shorts.
cards.challenge: Why do these peaks look so sharp and sudden?
cards.printAnswer: A fault lifted the range. Ice carved the horns. The valley floor sits close to the wall.

cards.label: Great Basin
cards.blurb: Great Basin — Wheeler Peak scenic drive and short alpine or cave options.
cards.challenge: Why can trees live thousands of years here?
cards.printAnswer: High, dry, and slow. Bristlecones grow a little each year and hold on in tough rock.

cards.label: Guadalupe
cards.blurb: Guadalupe Mountains — visitor center and short desert foothill walks.
cards.challenge: What was this mountain when it was under the sea?
cards.printAnswer: An ancient reef. The sea left, and the reef became a mountain of limestone.

cards.label: Hot Springs
cards.blurb: Hot Springs — Bathhouse Row and a short mountain trail or overlook.
cards.challenge: Why is the water hot coming out of the ground?
cards.printAnswer: Rain soaks deep, hits hot rock, and rises again. People built bathhouses on the springs.

cards.label: Ind. Dunes
cards.blurb: Indiana Dunes — lake beach and dune trail near Chicago.
cards.challenge: How do dunes form on a lake, not an ocean?
cards.printAnswer: Wind pushes beach sand inland. Plants grab it, and the piles grow along the shore.

cards.label: Isle Royale
cards.blurb: Isle Royale — wilderness island; ferry required, multi-day for most.
cards.challenge: Why is this park mostly reached by boat?
cards.printAnswer: It’s an island in a huge cold lake. Water protects the quiet and the wolves and moose.

cards.label: Joshua Tree
cards.blurb: Joshua Tree — desert gardens and rock piles; short loops near the visitor center.
cards.challenge: Why do Joshua trees look so spiky?
cards.printAnswer: They’re yuccas built for dry heat. Spikes save water and make shade in tiny pieces.

video.title: Joshua Tree boulders and night sky

cards.label: Kings Canyon
cards.blurb: Kings Canyon — Grant Grove big trees; pair carefully with Sequoia.
cards.challenge: Why is this canyon so deep?
cards.printAnswer: A river and old ice cut granite. The walls stay steep because the rock is tough.

cards.label: Lassen
cards.blurb: Lassen — hydrothermal boardwalks and peak views when road is open.
cards.challenge: What clues show a volcano is still around?
cards.printAnswer: Steam vents, hot ground, and a big peak. The mountain is quieter now, but the heat is still under it.

cards.label: Mammoth Cave
cards.blurb: Mammoth Cave — visitor center and a timed cave tour; surface trails optional.
cards.challenge: How can a cave be hundreds of miles long?
cards.printAnswer: Limestone and water. Passages join like underground streets on many levels.

cards.label: Mesa Verde
cards.blurb: Mesa Verde — cliff dwelling overlooks; many tours need tickets.
cards.challenge: Why build homes in a cliff?
cards.printAnswer: Overhangs shade and shelter. People farmed the mesa top and lived in the alcove.

cards.label: N. Cascades
cards.blurb: North Cascades — highway overlooks and short lakeside stops.
cards.challenge: Why are these mountains so jagged?
cards.printAnswer: Ice chewed the peaks. What’s left are sharp horns and hanging glaciers.

cards.label: New River
cards.blurb: New River Gorge — canyon rim overlooks and bridge views.
cards.challenge: Is the New River actually new?
cards.printAnswer: The name is old and a little backwards — the river is ancient. It cut a deep gorge through the plateau.

video.title: New River Gorge bridge and gorge

cards.label: Petrified
cards.blurb: Petrified Forest — painted desert views and short fossil wood loops.
cards.challenge: How does wood turn to stone?
cards.printAnswer: Trees buried in mud. Minerals soak in and copy the wood, cell by cell.

cards.label: Pinnacles
cards.blurb: Pinnacles — rock spires and short cave or bench trails; one entrance.
cards.challenge: Where did these pointy rocks come from?
cards.printAnswer: An old volcano. The mountain split and moved. What’s left are spires and caves.

cards.label: Rainier
cards.blurb: Mount Rainier — Paradise or Sunrise wildflower/views; one entrance only.
cards.challenge: Why does this mountain wear a white hat all year?
cards.printAnswer: It’s tall and cold. Snow piles into glaciers that creep down the sides.

cards.label: Redwood
cards.blurb: Redwoods — tall-tree groves and short understory walks.
cards.challenge: Why are redwoods so tall?
cards.printAnswer: Fog drips water onto the needles. They grow toward light for centuries.

cards.label: Saguaro
cards.blurb: Saguaro — giant cactus forest loops near Tucson; two districts, pick one.
cards.challenge: How does a cactus store water in a desert?
cards.printAnswer: Pleats expand like an accordion. Spines shade the skin and slow the wind.

cards.label: Sand Dunes
cards.blurb: Great Sand Dunes — dune field edge and Medano Creek when flowing.
cards.challenge: How did sand piles get so tall next to mountains?
cards.printAnswer: Wind drops sand when it hits the range. The piles grow into the tallest dunes in North America.

video.title: Great Sand Dunes against the mountains

cards.label: Sequoia
cards.blurb: Giant Forest short loops — enormous trees without a wilderness epic.
cards.challenge: How can a tree get this thick?
cards.printAnswer: It adds a ring every year for thousands of years. Fire can hollow it and it still lives.

cards.label: Shenandoah
cards.blurb: Shenandoah — Skyline Drive overlooks and one short waterfall or trail.
cards.challenge: Why do these mountains look soft and blue?
cards.printAnswer: They’re old and worn. Haze and distance turn ridges blue from Skyline Drive.

cards.label: T. Roosevelt
cards.blurb: Theodore Roosevelt — South Unit scenic drive and prairie dog towns.
cards.challenge: What carved these North Dakota badlands?
cards.printAnswer: The Little Missouri and weather. Soft rock cuts fast into buttes and valleys.

cards.label: Voyageurs
cards.blurb: Voyageurs — water park; visitor center and short shore trails without a boat.
cards.challenge: Why is this park a maze of lakes?
cards.printAnswer: Ice gouged the rock. Water filled the scratches, so you travel more by boat than by trail.

cards.label: White Sands
cards.blurb: White Sands — dune drive and sled hills of gypsum sand.
cards.challenge: Why is the sand white, not yellow?
cards.printAnswer: It’s gypsum, not beach quartz. The crystals stay bright and cool on your feet.

cards.label: Wind Cave
cards.blurb: Wind Cave — cave tour plus prairie wildlife above ground.
cards.challenge: What’s special about the cave’s boxwork?
cards.printAnswer: Thin fins of harder rock stick out of the walls. Wind and water left a honeycomb.

cards.label: Zion
cards.blurb: Zion Canyon shuttle corridor — red walls and riverside paths, not the full Narrows hike.
cards.challenge: How did a river cut such tall red walls?
cards.printAnswer: The Virgin River cut down through sandstone. The walls stay steep because the rock is stacked.
